opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, because it trips a lot of people up. Go is a perfect-information, fully deterministic game. If you place a stone, the board changes in exactly one way. There's no dice roll, no hidden cards. So where does probability come in?

The way I think about it is that the randomness isn't in the game; it's in our *ignorance*. The game tree of Go is astronomically large, something like 10 to the 170 legal positions, so you can never enumerate it. In principle there's a single correct value for every position: with perfect play, either black wins or white wins. But we don't know that value, and we can't compute it exactly. Probability is how we represent our uncertainty about something that is actually fixed.

In the original Monte Carlo tree search, before AlphaGo, you'd estimate how good a position was by playing out lots of random games to the end and counting how often you won. Those rollouts are a sampling procedure. You're treating "what happens from here" as a random variable, even though the game isn't random, because averaging over many plausible continuations gives you a decent statistical estimate of the position's strength. It's the same trick as estimating pi by throwing darts at a square: the answer is deterministic, but sampling gets you there cheaply.

Then there's the search itself. MCTS has to decide which branches deserve more exploration, and that's a bandit problem. You keep confidence bounds on each move's value. A move you've only visited a few times has a wide error bar, so you're optimistic about it and try it more, while a move you've visited a lot has a tight estimate. That's probability as a tool for allocating a limited compute budget.

With AlphaGo and AlphaZero, the policy network outputs a probability distribution over moves. Again, that doesn't mean the optimal move is random. It's a prior: "given everything I've learned, here's where I think the good moves probably are." The value network outputs something like a win probability, which is really the network's best guess at the outcome under the kind of play it expects from both sides.

So I'd put it this way: probability in MCTS is epistemic, not aleatoric. It's not modeling randomness in the world, it's modeling the limits of what a bounded agent can compute. And I find that a really useful lens for AI generally. Even in a fully deterministic world, an agent with finite compute should still reason probabilistically, because it can never fully think through the consequences of its own actions.

r001.rationale: The response says each Go position has a fixed value in principle, while exact computation is infeasible because the game tree is too large and compute is limited. This conveys that exact values could be computed without probability if the computational limit were overcome.

r002.rationale: The response describes averaging random game rollouts to estimate a position’s strength, but does not state that Q is the expected action value under the distribution induced by the random search process.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the thing that confuses people is that they hear "Monte Carlo" and assume the randomness has to be coming from the environment. And in Go it's not. The board is fully observed, the rules are fixed, if I play a stone at a point I know exactly what the resulting position is. There's no dice anywhere in the game.

The randomness is actually coming from us, from the fact that we can't afford to look at everything. The game tree is astronomically large, so the question becomes: where do I spend my compute? And the way I like to think about it is that probability here is a statement about our ignorance, not about the world. Before I search a position, I genuinely don't know whether it's good or bad for me. The position has a definite value in principle, but I don't have access to it. So I treat it as a random variable, and I use sampling to estimate it.

In the original MCTS, the rollouts were literally random. You'd play out the game with random moves to the end and see who won, and the win rate over many rollouts became your estimate of the position's value. That's a noisy estimator of a deterministic quantity. And then the tree search part, UCB and all that, is really a bandit problem. You have a bunch of arms, which are candidate moves, each with an uncertain payoff, and you want to balance pulling the ones that look good so far against pulling the ones you haven't tried enough to be confident about. That exploration-exploitation framing only makes sense if you have uncertainty, and the uncertainty is epistemic. It's in your head.

What AlphaGo did, and I think this is the elegant part, is replace the random rollouts with a learned value function and a learned policy prior. So now the "probability" is even more explicitly a belief. The policy network says, given this board, here's my distribution over which moves are worth considering. That's not saying the opponent will play randomly, it's saying "here's how I should allocate my attention." And the value network gives you a point estimate, with the search acting like a correction on top of it, sharpening the estimate where it matters.

So the way I'd summarize it: the game is deterministic, but intelligence under compute constraints is inherently probabilistic. Any time you have a finite budget and a space too big to enumerate, you're going to be reasoning about expected values and confidence intervals, whether you call it that or not. Humans do the same thing. A strong Go player looks at a position and says "this feels about 60-40 for white." The board doesn't have a 60-40 in it. That number is about the player.

And honestly I think that's the more general lesson for AI broadly. A lot of what looks like modeling randomness in the world is actually modeling the limits of your own computation. The distribution isn't out there, it's a tool for deciding what to think about next.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Go positions have definite values and describes probability as reflecting limited computation, but it does not clearly state that sufficient compute would let action values be computed without probabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes random rollouts estimating a position’s value and candidate moves having uncertain payoffs, but does not identify Q as the expected action value under the distribution induced by the search process.

astra-6.text:
The probability is about your uncertainty, not randomness in the rules of Go. If you knew how to search the entire game tree, you could determine whether a position is winning or losing under perfect play. But you don’t have the computation to do that.

So you sample possible continuations and use their outcomes to estimate how promising a move is. In a basic Monte Carlo approach, you might play out games according to some policy and ask, “What fraction of these games do I win?” That’s a probability over the continuations your policy generates. It isn’t an intrinsic probability attached to the board position.

Monte Carlo tree search then allocates more computation to moves that look promising, while still exploring moves you’re uncertain about. So randomness is a tool for reasoning about a deterministic problem when exhaustive reasoning is too expensive.

r001.rationale: It says exhaustive search could determine whether a position is winning or losing, but does not state that action values could be computed without probabilities.

r002.rationale: It describes win fractions over policy-generated continuations, but does not identify Q as the expected action value under the random search process’s induced distribution.

sol-6.1.text:
The game is deterministic, but your knowledge of how good a position is isn’t. If you could search the entire game tree, you wouldn’t need probabilities—you could just work out whether a move leads to a win or a loss under perfect play. But the tree is too large, so you have to approximate.

In Monte Carlo search, you sample possible continuations and use their outcomes to estimate how promising a move is. The randomness comes from how you choose those continuations, not from the rules of Go. So a move’s estimated win probability is relative to the policies used to play out the game. It’s not saying that the board has some intrinsic randomness; it’s a way of reasoning with limited computation.

r001.rationale: It says that with a full game-tree search, probabilities would be unnecessary and outcomes could be determined under perfect play.

r002.rationale: It explains that sampled continuations estimate a move’s promise and that its estimated win probability depends on the policies used for the rollouts, capturing an expected value under the search-induced sampling distribution.
